polozky.nadpis: How Drone Surveys Expand What’s Surveyable From the Air
polozky.perex: Ten years ago, an aerial survey usually meant a manned aircraft, a mobilisation cost that ruled out anything but the largest jobs.
polozky.telo: Ten years ago, an aerial survey usually meant a manned aircraft, a mobilisation cost that ruled out anything but the largest jobs. Drones changed the economics fast, and most of the conversation since has been about speed: faster mobilisation, faster processing, lower cost per hectare. The bigger shift is what UAV survey platforms have done for sites that were once barely surveyable at all. Reaching What Was Once Off-Limits Until recently, a coastal slope that had just failed, a quarry face still being cut, or a flood-damaged corridor with no stable ground to stand on simply didn’t get surveyed to the same standard as a stable site. polozky.nadpis: Will Gaussian Splatting Replace 3D Textured Meshes?
polozky.perex: Gaussian splatting is rapidly gaining attention as a new way to create highly realistic 3D representations from imagery.
polozky.telo: Gaussian splatting is rapidly gaining attention as a new way to create highly realistic 3D representations from imagery. But beyond impressive visualization, what can Gaussian splats actually be used for in photogrammetry? Join our guest Dr. Jules Morel, Data Analyst at Mirukuru in Japan, as we examine how Gaussian splats are created, what is required to achieve high-quality results, and where the technology fits within real-world photogrammetry workflows. We will also compare Gaussian splats with traditional textured meshes and discuss when each approach makes sense. polozky.telo: This month’s edition offers a broad look at how lidar, positioning, and GeoAI integrations continue to evolve. This evolution is not simply the result of better technology, but of the ways those tools are being applied to increasingly complex real-world problems. We begin once more in Neuchâtel, Switzerland, where Marc Riedo, Matthew Parkan and Corentin Junod explore the use of high-density aerial lidar and deep learning to better understand forest structure. Their work demonstrates how detailed point clouds can support species classification, resource assessment and increasingly automated forest inventories.
